Stage 2: Accept the orderits process steps, outcomes and measures

Before you start: the access you need

You need to be able to read each of these. A check you cannot run is a gap in this runbook: note it.

  • Order Processor: Grace-period releases published; Order Processor exits and restarts; Grace-period poll query failures; Grace period and poll interval in effect; Event bus start failures
  • Event bus: Bindings on exchange eshop_event_bus; Broker running; Broker resource alarms and headroom
  • Ordering API: Queue Ordering: messages waiting and consumers; Ordering API messages it failed to handle; Ordering API messages of an event type it does not know; Ordering API transaction failures, by command; Ordering outbox rows not published, by State; Ordering API publish failures
  • Catalog API: Queue Catalog: messages waiting and consumers; Catalog API messages it failed to handle; Catalog outbox rows by State; Catalog API publish failures
  • Order: Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state; Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
  • Ordering database: Ordering database accepting connections; Long-running statements on orderingdb; Connections to the postgres server against max_connections
  • Catalog database: Catalog database accepting connections; Long-running statements on catalogdb; Connections to the postgres server from catalogdb
  • Payment Processor: Payment Processor messages it failed to handle; Payment results published, by kind; Queue PaymentProcessor: messages waiting and consumers
  • Deployment, configuration and restart history for Order Processor, Ordering API, Catalog API, Payment Processor, ClientApp, Mobile BFF, Identity API.
Every check

Is Event bus down or unreachable?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Event busReads Broker running
How to check

In the eventbus container (az containerapp exec --name eventbus --resource-group <rg>) run:

rabbitmq-diagnostics -q ping
Not the cause if Ping succeeded
The cause if no answer
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 1
Why this check reads it this way
The broker does not answer: the poll's publish throws and ends Order Processor, Ordering API's and Catalog API's post-commit publishes are marked failed, and Payment Processor's result is lost. Orders in Submitted are released once the broker is back and order-processor restarted; those in Awaiting validation or Stock confirmed are stranded. Messages already queued wait only if the broker keeps its data: the AppHost gives it no data volume

Are Ordering database and Catalog database down or unreachable?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Ordering database and Catalog databaseReads Ordering database accepting connections; Catalog database accepting connections
How to check

In the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run:

for db in orderingdb catalogdb; do echo $db; pg_isready -d $db; done
Not the cause if accepting connections under both names
The cause if no response, or rejecting connections, under either name
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 1
Why this check reads it this way
The ordering or the catalog database does not answer; both are on one postgres server with identitydb and webhooksdb. The poll's query fails and returns nothing, so orders in Submitted wait and move on once it is back; Ordering API's status changes and Catalog API's stock check fail on messages already acknowledged, so orders in Awaiting validation or Stock confirmed are stranded

Is Event bus slow?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Event busReads Broker resource alarms and headroom; Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state
How to check

In the eventbus container (az containerapp exec --name eventbus --resource-group <rg>) run:

rabbitmq-diagnostics check_local_alarms

Memory and disk free against their watermarks in rabbitmqctl status.

Not the cause if no alarms, memory and disk well inside their limits
The cause if no alarm yet, but memory or disk close to its watermark
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Can’t restore here: escalate to the owner of Event bus
Why this check reads it this way
The broker slows publishing connections when its queues cannot keep up; memory or disk nearing its watermark is a leading sign of the alarm in the check “Is Event bus full or out of capacity?”. Messages arrive late and the orders move late

Is Event bus full or out of capacity?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Event busReads Broker resource alarms and headroom; Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state
How to check

In the eventbus container (az containerapp exec --name eventbus --resource-group <rg>) run:

rabbitmq-diagnostics check_local_alarms
Not the cause if no alarms
The cause if a memory or disk alarm in effect
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Can’t restore here: escalate to the owner of Event bus
Why this check reads it this way
A memory or disk alarm makes the broker block publishing connections until it clears; the code sets no publish timeout, so the moves resume late rather than fail

Are Ordering database and Catalog database slow?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Ordering database and Catalog databaseReads Long-running statements on orderingdb; Long-running statements on catalogdb; Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state
How to check

In the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run:

psql -U postgres -d orderingdb

Then:

SELECT datname, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname IN ('orderingdb','catalogdb') AND state = 'active' AND now() - query_start > interval '5 seconds' GROUP BY datname;
Not the cause if no rows
The cause if a row for either database, persisting
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Can’t restore here: escalate to the owner of each part that matched
Why this check reads it this way
Statements run long on the ordering or the catalog database: the poll, the status writes, the outbox writes and the stock lookups finish late, and orders leave late. A statement that fails outright shows as the unavailable test instead

Are Ordering database and Catalog database full or out of capacity?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Ordering database and Catalog databaseReads Connections to the postgres server against max_connections; Connections to the postgres server from catalogdb
How to check

In the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run:

psql -U postgres -d orderingdb

Then:

SELECT datname, count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity GROUP BY datname;
SHOW max_connections;
Not the cause if the total well below max_connections
The cause if the total at max_connections; the rows show which database holds the connections
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 1
Why this check reads it this way
The shared postgres server refuses new connections: the poll's query fails and orders in Submitted wait; status changes and stock checks fail on messages already acknowledged, stranding orders in Awaiting validation or Stock confirmed

Are Ordering API and Catalog API not running, leaving their messages queued?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Ordering API and Catalog APIReads Queue Ordering: messages waiting and consumers; Queue Catalog: messages waiting and consumers; Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state
How to check

In the eventbus container (az containerapp exec --name eventbus --resource-group <rg>) run rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages consumers, and read the rows for queues Ordering and Catalog: each row names its queue, and so the service that matched.

Not the cause if consumers 1 or more on both rows
The cause if consumers 0, with messages waiting, on either row
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 3
Why this check reads it this way
The consumer of Ordering API (queue Ordering) or of Catalog API (queue Catalog) is not attached: the service is down, or its bus start returned without consuming because the connection was not open or setup failed, and nothing retries it. Messages wait in the durable queue as persistent messages and are handled when it returns, so the orders leave late

Is Order Processor not polling?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by statePart Order ProcessorReads Grace-period releases published; Order Processor exits and restarts
How to check

Read the last 300 lines of order-processor's console log (az containerapp logs show --name order-processor --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for lines 'Publishing integration event:', and its system log for exits:

az containerapp logs show --name order-processor --resource-group <rg> --type system
Not the cause if A 'Publishing integration event:' line every 30 seconds for each Submitted order past 1 minute; no exits
The cause if No such lines, and the container exited or is not running
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 2
Why this check reads it this way
Order Processor is not running, or its background service has ended: an exception from a publish is not caught in the poll loop, and .NET's default for a failed background service is to stop the host. No order leaves Submitted

Are Ordering API and Catalog API falling behind on their queues?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Ordering API and Catalog APIReads Queue Ordering: messages waiting and consumers; Queue Catalog: messages waiting and consumers; Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state
How to check

In the eventbus container (az containerapp exec --name eventbus --resource-group <rg>) run rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages consumers, and read the rows for queues Ordering and Catalog, twice, a minute apart.

Not the cause if messages near 0 and not growing on both rows
The cause if messages growing on either row while its consumers is 1 or more
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 6
Why this check reads it this way
Ordering API handles its queue on one consumer, one message at a time, and the stock answers and the payment-succeeded answer each wait 10 seconds first. Above about six such answers a minute per instance the queue grows; every 30 seconds the poll adds another release message for each order still Submitted, feeding it. Catalog API also handles queue Catalog on a single consumer, so stock requests arriving faster than it answers wait there

Is Order Processor's poll query failing?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by statePart Order ProcessorReads Grace-period poll query failures
How to check

Search the console log of order-processor (az containerapp logs show --name order-processor --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for 'Error querying confirmed grace period orders after grace period'.

Not the cause if No such line
The cause if The line every 30 seconds
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 5
Why this check reads it this way
The poll's query fails (database unreachable, credentials): the error is logged, an empty list is returned and the loop goes on, so nothing is released

Is Order Processor polling but missing cases?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by statePart Order ProcessorReads Grace period and poll interval in effect
How to check

Read BackgroundTaskOptions__GracePeriodTime and BackgroundTaskOptions__CheckUpdateTime in order-processor's configuration (az containerapp show --name order-processor --resource-group <rg>), else the shipped appsettings.json.

Not the cause if 1 and 30 (the shipped values)
The cause if A different value, larger than the age of the held orders allows
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 7
Why this check reads it this way
The poll selects by its own settings: GracePeriodTime in minutes and CheckUpdateTime in seconds. A changed or mis-entered value (seconds written as minutes) holds orders in Submitted while the poller runs and logs normally

Is Order Processor failing to publish its messages?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by statePart Order ProcessorReads Event bus start failures; Grace-period releases published
How to check

Search the console log of order-processor (az containerapp logs show --name order-processor --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for 'Error starting RabbitMQ connection' at its last start, and for the service ending just after a 'Publishing integration event:' line.

Not the cause if Neither
The cause if Either one
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 4
Why this check reads it this way
The publish of GracePeriodConfirmedIntegrationEvent throws. The configured retry does not retry it, because Execute runs an async lambda. The exception escapes the poll loop and ends the service, as in the check “Is Order Processor not polling?” (Polly's Execute overloads: https://www.pollydocs.org/api/Polly.ResiliencePipeline.html: an async lambda binds to Execute<TResult>(Func<TResult>), so the pipeline only sees the returned task)

Are the messages for Event bus accepted but routed to no queue?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by statePart Event busReads Bindings on exchange eshop_event_bus
How to check

In the eventbus container (az containerapp exec --name eventbus --resource-group <rg>) run rabbitmqctl list_bindings source_name destination_name routing_key, and read the rows whose source is eshop_event_bus.

Not the cause if eshop_event_bus Ordering GracePeriodConfirmedIntegrationEvent is listed
The cause if That binding is missing
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 3
Why this check reads it this way
GracePeriodConfirmedIntegrationEvent reaches queue Ordering only through a binding Ordering API makes at its start. It is published mandatory but nothing handles returned messages, so without the binding it is dropped. The next poll publishes again

Are Ordering API and Catalog API failing on the messages they read?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Ordering API and Catalog APIReads Ordering API messages it failed to handle; Ordering API messages of an event type it does not know; Catalog API messages it failed to handle
How to check

For each of ordering-api and catalog-api, search its console log (az containerapp logs show --name <app> --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for 'Unable to resolve event type for event name', or for 'Error Processing message' carrying a JSON or type error with no 'Error Handling transaction for' line beside it, whose quoted message body carries the OrderId of one of these orders (the line quotes the body but names no event). Note which service logged it.

Not the cause if Neither, in either service
The cause if Either, for these orders; the service whose log holds it is the one that matched
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 1
Why this check reads it this way
Ordering API cannot read a release, stock or payment answer, or Catalog API cannot read a stock request: an unknown event name is logged and dropped, and a body that does not deserialize throws; either way the message is acknowledged and gone. An order still in Submitted is sent again by the next poll and moves on; one in Awaiting validation or Stock confirmed is stranded, because the poll re-sends only for Submitted

Is the act failing inside Ordering API and Catalog API?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Ordering API and Catalog APIReads Ordering API transaction failures, by command; Catalog API messages it failed to handle
How to check

Search the console log of ordering-api (az containerapp logs show --name ordering-api --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for 'Error Handling transaction for' followed by SetAwaitingValidationOrderStatusCommand, SetStockConfirmedOrderStatusCommand, SetStockRejectedOrderStatusCommand, SetPaidOrderStatusCommand or CancelOrderCommand, and the console log of catalog-api the same way for 'Error Processing message' whose exception is a database (Npgsql) error. Note which service logged it.

Not the cause if No such line in either service
The cause if Lines for these orders; the service whose log holds them is the one that matched
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 1
Why this check reads it this way
Ordering API's status change throws and its transaction rolls back, or Catalog API's stock check throws reading an item or saving its answer row. The message was already acknowledged, so the order stays where it was: one in Submitted is sent again by the next poll, one in Awaiting validation or Stock confirmed is stranded

Are changes in Ordering API left unpublished in its outbox?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Ordering APIReads Ordering outbox rows not published, by State
How to check

In the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run:

psql -U postgres -d orderingdb

Then:

SELECT o."Id", o."OrderStatus", l."State", l."EventId" FROM ordering.orders o LEFT JOIN ordering."IntegrationEventLog" l ON (l."Content"::jsonb ->> 'OrderId')::int = o."Id" AND ((o."OrderStatus" = 'AwaitingValidation' AND l."EventTypeName" LIKE '%OrderStatusChangedToAwaitingValidationIntegrationEvent') OR (o."OrderStatus" = 'StockConfirmed' AND l."EventTypeName" LIKE '%OrderStatusChangedToStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent')) WHERE o."OrderStatus" IN ('AwaitingValidation','StockConfirmed') AND now() - o."OrderDate" > interval '2 minutes';
Not the cause if "State" 2 (Published) on every row
The cause if "State" 0 (NotPublished) or 1 (InProgress)
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 1
Why this check reads it this way
The status and its outbox row commit together, and the row is published only by the same request right after the commit. A crash or lost connection in between leaves it at State 0, or 1 if it died mid-publish, and nothing sends it later

Are changes in Catalog API left unpublished in its outbox?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by statePart Catalog APIReads Catalog outbox rows by State
How to check

In the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run:

psql -U postgres -d catalogdb

Then:

SELECT "State", "EventTypeName", "CreationTime" FROM "IntegrationEventLog" WHERE ("Content"::jsonb ->> 'OrderId')::int IN (<ids of the aged AwaitingValidation orders>);
Not the cause if one row per order at "State" 2 (Published)
The cause if a row at "State" 0 (NotPublished) or 1 (InProgress)
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 1
Why this check reads it this way
Catalog API saves its answer row in a transaction, then publishes it in the same handler. A crash in between leaves it at State 0 or 1, and nothing sends it later

Are the messages for Event bus accepted but routed to no queue?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Event busReads Bindings on exchange eshop_event_bus
How to check

In the eventbus container (az containerapp exec --name eventbus --resource-group <rg>) run rabbitmqctl list_bindings source_name destination_name routing_key, and read the rows whose source is eshop_event_bus.

Not the cause if Catalog bound for OrderStatusChangedToAwaitingValidationIntegrationEvent; PaymentProcessor for OrderStatusChangedToStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent; Ordering for OrderStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent, OrderStockRejectedIntegrationEvent, OrderPaymentSucceededIntegrationEvent and OrderPaymentFailedIntegrationEvent
The cause if One of those bindings missing
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 1
Why this check reads it this way
No queue is bound for the stock or payment request or its answer, so the broker drops it. The outbox row still shows 2 (Published)

Are Ordering API and Catalog API failing to publish their messages?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Ordering API and Catalog APIReads Ordering API publish failures; Catalog API publish failures
How to check

Search the console log of ordering-api (az containerapp logs show --name ordering-api --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for 'Error publishing integration event:', and that of catalog-api the same way for 'Error Publishing integration event:', and read the exception each carries. Note which service logged it.

Not the cause if No such line in either service
The cause if Lines for these orders' events naming a broker or connection error; the service whose log holds them is the one that matched
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 1
Why this check reads it this way
Ordering API or Catalog API cannot hand the event to the broker; the retry does not apply (EventBusRabbitMQ/RabbitMQEventBus.cs:57; Polly's Execute overloads: https://www.pollydocs.org/api/Polly.ResiliencePipeline.html: an async lambda binds to Execute<TResult>(Func<TResult>), so the pipeline only sees the returned task), and the failure is caught, logged with the broker's exception and the outbox row marked failed

Are Ordering API's outbox rows marked failed?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Ordering APIReads Ordering outbox rows not published, by State; Ordering API publish failures
How to check

In the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run:

psql -U postgres -d orderingdb

Then:

SELECT o."Id", o."OrderStatus", l."State", l."EventId" FROM ordering.orders o LEFT JOIN ordering."IntegrationEventLog" l ON (l."Content"::jsonb ->> 'OrderId')::int = o."Id" AND ((o."OrderStatus" = 'AwaitingValidation' AND l."EventTypeName" LIKE '%OrderStatusChangedToAwaitingValidationIntegrationEvent') OR (o."OrderStatus" = 'StockConfirmed' AND l."EventTypeName" LIKE '%OrderStatusChangedToStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent')) WHERE o."OrderStatus" IN ('AwaitingValidation','StockConfirmed') AND now() - o."OrderDate" > interval '2 minutes';

Then search the console log of ordering-api (az containerapp logs show --name ordering-api --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for 'Error publishing integration event:' with those EventIds.

Not the cause if "State" 2 (Published) on every row
The cause if "State" 3 (PublishedFailed), with the error line
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 1
Why this check reads it this way
The publish threw: the row is set to 3 and the error logged, and no code tries it again

Are Catalog API's outbox rows marked failed?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by statePart Catalog APIReads Catalog outbox rows by State; Catalog API publish failures
How to check

In the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run:

psql -U postgres -d catalogdb

Then:

SELECT "State", "EventTypeName", "CreationTime" FROM "IntegrationEventLog" WHERE ("Content"::jsonb ->> 'OrderId')::int IN (<ids of the aged AwaitingValidation orders>);

Then search the console log of catalog-api (az containerapp logs show --name catalog-api --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for 'Error Publishing integration event:'.

Not the cause if "State" 2 (Published)
The cause if "State" 3 (PublishedFailed), with the error line
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 1
Why this check reads it this way
Catalog API's publish threw: the row is set to 3 and the error logged; nothing tries again

Is Payment Processor not running, leaving its messages queued?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Payment ProcessorReads Queue PaymentProcessor: messages waiting and consumers; Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state
How to check

In the eventbus container (az containerapp exec --name eventbus --resource-group <rg>) run rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages consumers, and read the row for queue PaymentProcessor.

Not the cause if consumers 1 or more
The cause if consumers 0, with messages waiting
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 3
Why this check reads it this way
Payment Processor's consumer is not attached (as the check “Are Ordering API and Catalog API not running, leaving their messages queued?”); requests wait in queue PaymentProcessor

Is Payment Processor falling behind on its queue?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Payment ProcessorReads Queue PaymentProcessor: messages waiting and consumers; Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state
How to check

In the eventbus container (az containerapp exec --name eventbus --resource-group <rg>) run rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages consumers, and read the row for queue PaymentProcessor, twice, a minute apart.

Not the cause if messages near 0
The cause if messages growing while consumers is 1 or more
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 6
Why this check reads it this way
Payment requests arrive faster than Payment Processor's single consumer handles them

Is Payment Processor failing to publish its messages?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Payment ProcessorReads Payment Processor messages it failed to handle; Payment results published, by kind
How to check

Search the console log of payment-processor (az containerapp logs show --name payment-processor --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for 'Publishing integration event:' for the order followed by 'Error Processing message' for its OrderStatusChangedToStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent.

Not the cause if A 'Publishing integration event:' line and no error
The cause if The publishing line followed by 'Error Processing message'
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 1
Why this check reads it this way
Payment Processor publishes its result with no outbox and no working retry; the exception leaves the handler and the request message is acknowledged and gone (Polly's Execute overloads: https://www.pollydocs.org/api/Polly.ResiliencePipeline.html: an async lambda binds to Execute<TResult>(Func<TResult>), so the pipeline only sees the returned task)

Is Payment Processor failing on the messages it reads?

Used by Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Payment ProcessorReads Payment Processor messages it failed to handle
How to check

Search the console log of payment-processor (az containerapp logs show --name payment-processor --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for 'Error Processing message' for OrderStatusChangedToStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent with no 'Publishing integration event:' line before it.

Not the cause if No such line
The cause if The error with no result published
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 1
Why this check reads it this way
Payment Processor cannot read the request (unknown event name, or a body that does not deserialize); acknowledged and gone; no result is published

Is Payment Processor completing the act, but wrongly?

Used by Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Payment ProcessorReads Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
How to check

Read PaymentOptions__PaymentSucceeded in payment-processor's configuration (az containerapp show --name payment-processor --resource-group <rg>), else the shipped PaymentProcessor/appsettings.json.

Not the cause if true, or not set (the shipped value is true)
The cause if false
‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: remedy 13
Why this check reads it this way
The payment decision fails orders that should pass: the setting PaymentOptions:PaymentSucceeded decides every payment and reads false, so every order reaching Stock confirmed is cancelled (“The order is cancelled because payment failed”) and none of them waits. Orders paid with no money moving are counted by “Orders marked paid with no payment taken”
Causes the design rules out, so no check is needed
  • Ordering API, the act completes wrongly: the move writes only the new status and an outbox row built from the order's own items, and acts only from Submitted
  • Ordering API, relay not running: there is no relay process; the request that commits the status publishes its rows itself. What it leaves behind is the check “Are changes in Ordering API left unpublished in its outbox?” and the check “Are Ordering API's outbox rows marked failed?”
  • Catalog API, relay not running: no relay; the handler publishes its own row at once
  • Catalog API, the act completes wrongly: as a cause of orders held past the time limit. A product the catalogue does not hold is skipped and the order confirmed, and a stock check reserves nothing: wrong, but the order moves on. Counted by “Orders confirmed with an unknown item” at process step 2.2
  • Ordering API, the act completes wrongly: as a cause of orders held past the time limit. The stock and payment setters act only from their expected state and otherwise change nothing, and a cancellation of an order already Cancelled sets it Cancelled again, so a late or repeated answer leaves the order out of the stage or where another move put it
  • Payment Processor, the act fails: the decision reads one setting and nothing before the publish can throw; a publish failure is the check “Is Payment Processor failing to publish its messages?”
  • Ordering API, callee down: as a cause of orders held past the time limit. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: Ordering API down, so Mobile BFF cannot reach it
  • Mobile BFF, callee down: as a cause of orders held past the time limit. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: Mobile BFF down, so the app cannot reach it
  • Ordering API, callee returns an error: as a cause of orders held past the time limit. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: Ordering API answers 500 'Cancel order failed to process.'
  • Ordering API, callee slow or hangs: as a cause of orders held past the time limit. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: the cancel is slow; the main path is not waiting on it
  • ClientApp, caller gives up mid-call: as a cause of orders held past the time limit. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: the app gives up; if Ordering API finished the cancel, the order is Cancelled and leaves the stage
  • Ordering API, the act fails: as a cause of orders held past the time limit. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: the cancel command throws or returns false; a throw is caught by the identified-command wrapper, which returns false, so Ordering API reports the cancel failed with 500 'Cancel order failed to process.'
  • Ordering API, the act completes wrongly: a cancellation that lands while the release or the stock check is in flight leaves the order Cancelled, and the late message is ignored because each setter acts only from its expected state
  • Ordering API, the act completes wrongly: as a cause of orders held past the time limit. A cancellation while payment is in flight leaves the order Cancelled and the payment result ignored: wrong, and with a real gateway money taken for a cancelled order, but the order is out of the stage. Counted by “Orders cancelled while their payment went ahead”
  • Ordering database, unavailable: as a cause of orders held past the time limit. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: the ordering database for the cancel write; the same fault on the main path is the check “Are Ordering database and Catalog database down or unreachable?”, the check “Are Ordering database and Catalog database slow?” and the check “Are Ordering database and Catalog database full or out of capacity?”
  • Ordering database, slow: as a cause of orders held past the time limit. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: the ordering database for the cancel write; the same fault on the main path is the check “Are Ordering database and Catalog database down or unreachable?”, the check “Are Ordering database and Catalog database slow?” and the check “Are Ordering database and Catalog database full or out of capacity?”
  • Ordering database, full or out of capacity: as a cause of orders held past the time limit. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: the ordering database for the cancel write; the same fault on the main path is the check “Are Ordering database and Catalog database down or unreachable?”, the check “Are Ordering database and Catalog database slow?” and the check “Are Ordering database and Catalog database full or out of capacity?”
  • Identity API, unavailable: as a cause of orders held past the time limit. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: Identity API, whose keys Ordering API uses to check the customer's token; the main path carries no token
  • Identity API, slow: as a cause of orders held past the time limit. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: Identity API, whose keys Ordering API uses to check the customer's token; the main path carries no token
  • Identity API, full or out of capacity: as a cause of orders held past the time limit. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: Identity API, whose keys Ordering API uses to check the customer's token; the main path carries no token
  • Ordering API, callee answers wrongly: as a cause of orders held past the time limit or cancelled by a failure. The cancel call's answer is the result of the order's own cancel command: Ordering API answers 500 'Cancel order failed to process.' when the command fails, and OK when it succeeded or when its request id was seen before, even on a first attempt that failed. Either way the order stays on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancellation's own outcome is “Ordering API, the act completes wrongly”
  • Ordering database, answers stale or wrong: the ordering database is one postgres server with no replica or cache in front of it, so every read sees the last committed write
  • Catalog database, answers stale or wrong: the catalog database is a database on the same single postgres server, with no replica or cache in front of it
  • Event bus, answers stale or wrong: the broker carries the messages and answers no read a move decides on; a message lost, unrouted or late is tested by the message modes
  • Identity API, answers stale or wrong: as a cause of orders held past the time limit or cancelled by a failure. Ordering API requires the shopper's token on the cancel call, which Identity API issues; a stale or wrong answer from it fails the cancellation, which leaves the order on the main path, as in “Identity API, unavailable”
Restore

After any action that restores: go back to the entry of the alert that fired and run its checks again for every case still affected, since a restore can leave cases in other states.

Remedy 1: re-drive

psql -U postgres -d orderingdb

Then:

SELECT "Id", "OrderStatus" FROM ordering.orders WHERE "OrderStatus" IN ('AwaitingValidation','StockConfirmed') AND now() - "OrderDate" > interval '2 minutes';

UPDATE ordering.orders SET "OrderStatus" = 'Submitted' WHERE "Id" IN (<ids>) AND "OrderStatus" IN ('AwaitingValidation','StockConfirmed');

What not to do.

  • Do not restart order-processor to move orders held in Awaiting validation or Stock confirmed: the poll selects only Submitted
  • Do not restart the postgres or eventbus container apps as a first move: no data volume is declared for either, so find out where their data lives first
  • Do not set "OrderStatus" straight to 'StockConfirmed', 'Paid' or 'Cancelled' by SQL: the events are raised only inside the setters, so no outbox row is written and nothing after it happens (payment, stock reduction, notifications)
  • Do not set an outbox row's "State" back to 0 to have it sent: nothing reads unsent rows after the request that wrote them
  • Do not look for failed messages to replay: a consumer acknowledges a message it failed on, and no dead-letter queue exists

Declare an incident when the operators’ severity definition says to: the register holds no trigger for it. Keep working the entry while it is declared. For that call, what is at stake here is below; the stage itself is Stage 2: Accept the order.

What is at stake.

  • Order id ("Id"): The only key that joins the order across services and to the customer
  • Order total (sum of Units x UnitPrice): Money the customer pays; value blocked while the order is stuck
  • Items and units (ordering."orderItems"): What must be in stock and shipped
  • Buyer (ordering.buyers "IdentityGuid"): Who is waiting and who is told
  • Delivery address: Where the goods must arrive
  • Payment method (card number masked to the last four digits): What is charged
  • Cannot be undone: The order is cancelled because an item is out of stock
  • Cannot be undone: Payment is taken for the order
  • Cannot be undone: The order is cancelled because payment failed
  • Cannot be undone: The order is cancelled at the customer's request
  • Customer experience and trust, if “The order is released for stock checking when the grace period ends” fails: counted in orders held in Submitted past the grace period. Every poll publishes again for orders still Submitted
  • Customer experience and trust, if “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order” fails: counted in orders stranded in Awaiting validation. A lost or failed message is not sent again; nothing polls Awaiting validation
  • Customer experience and trust, if “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order” fails: counted in orders confirmed with an item the catalogue does not hold. The check skips a product it cannot find, so the order is confirmed
  • Customer experience and trust, if “The order is cancelled because an item is out of stock” fails: counted in orders stranded in Awaiting validation after their stock was rejected. Same mechanism as process step 2.2
  • Customer experience and trust, if “Payment is taken for the order” fails: counted in orders stranded in Stock confirmed, not paid. A lost payment request or result is not sent again
  • Money directly at stake, if “Payment is taken for the order” fails: counted in order totals not collected for orders stranded in Stock confirmed. Value blocked: the order total is not taken while the order waits
  • Customer experience and trust, if “The order is cancelled because payment failed” fails: counted in orders stranded in Stock confirmed after a failed payment. Same mechanism as the expected outcome “Payment is taken for the order”
  • Customer experience and trust, if “The order is cancelled at the customer's request” fails: counted in cancel requests that fail, so the order goes ahead. The customer gets an error and must try again. A cancel that lands while payment is in flight leaves the order Cancelled and the payment result ignored; with a real gateway that would be money taken for a cancelled order

What to hand over: the alert and what it guards (its entry); the affected case ids by state; whether new cases are still affected now; which checks ran and what they showed; what was contained and what was done; the look-back time.

Close
EndingClose
Already knownLink the incident, then close.
Planned changeLink the window or change, then close. Note that the alert should have been suppressed, if it should.
Self-healedOnly for an alert that counts cases waiting: confirm it is back under its threshold, then close. Note that its threshold or window may be wrong.
RestoreAfter the action, confirm the alert is under its threshold, no case it counted is still affected, and new cases get through. Any that remain: back to its entry.
Can’t restore hereEscalate, and hand over.
None of the checks explains itEscalate with what you have, and note the gap in this runbook.
None of the checks explains it

For the cases no check explained: escalate them with what you have, and note the gap in this runbook (a cause it does not cover, or a check that could not be run). Then go on with the next group of cases that still has some: an unexplained group does not end the walk for the others.

Stage 2 runbook: Accept the order › Alert

Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state

No test of this runbook is on record.

An order still in Submitted, Awaiting validation or Stock confirmed past the time limit has not been accepted when the shopper expects, and the moves out of Awaiting validation and Stock confirmed strand it with nothing to move it again (lifecycle “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order”, “The order is cancelled because an item is out of stock”, “Payment is taken for the order” and “The order is cancelled because payment failed”, recovery stranded)

It has been above the operators’ threshold for longer than their window (the alert).

Its cases those held in the stage past the time limit. A case not past the time limit is not one of this alert's.
Look back from when the oldest of its cases entered the stage, to now. The alert fires only once a case has waited past the time limit, so its cause can be as old as that: never read a test over only the time since the count began rising.
Do now
  1. List its cases and set the look-back. Every check below runs on these cases, over that time. List them with the alert’s own count:
    How

    In the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run:

    psql -U postgres -d orderingdb
    SELECT "OrderStatus", count(*) FROM ordering.orders WHERE "OrderStatus" IN ('Submitted','AwaitingValidation','StockConfirmed') AND now() - "OrderDate" > interval '2 minutes' GROUP BY 1;

    The interval is the stage's time limit in the code, proposed.

  2. Contain. No hold is needed: the cases the alert counts are still in the stage, and nothing more is done to them while they wait.
  3. Do not restart order-processor to move orders held in Awaiting validation or Stock confirmed: the poll selects only Submitted
  4. Do not restart the postgres or eventbus container apps as a first move: no data volume is declared for either, so find out where their data lives first
  5. Do not set "OrderStatus" straight to 'StockConfirmed', 'Paid' or 'Cancelled' by SQL: the events are raised only inside the setters, so no outbox row is written and nothing after it happens (payment, stock reduction, notifications)
  6. Do not set an outbox row's "State" back to 0 to have it sent: nothing reads unsent rows after the request that wrote them
  7. Do not look for failed messages to replay: a consumer acknowledges a message it failed on, and no dead-letter queue exists
  8. Escalate or declare as soon as a trigger is met, at any point below. Triggers ›
Check first
1Is this already known?
How
Look for an open incident, or a known error with a fix in flight, for any of these parts: Order Processor, Ordering API, Ordering database, Event bus, Catalog API, Catalog database, Payment Processor, ClientApp, Mobile BFF, Identity API. Not the cause if there is none; the cause if one is open: link it and close.
Yes → Already known
2Was it planned?
How
Look for a maintenance window on any of those parts, or a planned change to a timing the stage depends on (Process step 2.1: The order is released for stock checking when the grace period ends — Grace period GracePeriodTime 1 minute, polled every CheckUpdateTime 30 seconds. Every run re-publishes for each order still Submitted. The bus's retry policy never retries a failed publish: Execute is given an async lambda, so the failure lands in the returned task, not the call; Process step 2.2: Stock is confirmed for every item of the order — 10 seconds of simulated work before the status is set. Ordering API consumes its queue with one consumer on one channel, so these waits queue behind one another; Other outcome: The order is cancelled because an item is out of stock — 10 seconds of simulated work before the status is set, queued behind the other waits as in “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order”; Expected outcome: Payment is taken for the order — 10 seconds of simulated work before the status is set, on the same single consumer as “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order”; Other outcome: The order is cancelled because payment failed — No wait and no timeout: unlike “Payment is taken for the order”, Ordering API sets Cancelled at once, but on the same single consumer as “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order”, so it queues behind the 10-second waits there. No clock watches a message waiting in its queue, and the queue sets no expiry; Other outcome: The order is cancelled at the customer's request — No timeout of its own: the mobile app's HttpClient has no handler, so it keeps .NET's default timeout of 100 seconds and makes one attempt; Mobile BFF's route and Ordering API's cancel endpoint set none, and the cancel itself waits for nothing). Not the cause if there is none; the cause if a window is open or a setting was changed on purpose: link it and close.
Yes → Planned change
3Did something change when it started?
How
Look for any deploy, configuration change or unplanned restart of those parts since the look-back time above. Not the cause if there is none; the cause if a change lines up with the start.
Yes → Roll the change back, or escalate to the owner of the part that changed
4Is it already recovering?
How
Read the alert's own count over one window (for a count of cases waiting, with the oldest only just past the time limit). Not the cause if it is not falling; it is recovering if the count falls within one window: confirm it is back under its threshold, then close.
Yes → Self-healed
Find the cause in order, on its cases only. No → next check. Yes → take its ending for the cases it lists, and go on for the rest. A check whose evidence lists no cases (a match in a log or a metric) explains no case by itself: note it, if the match falls inside the look-back, and go on; a case no later check explains takes the ending of every check noted for it, each named in the hand-over; where those endings differ, escalate rather than restore. A result you cannot read, or a check you cannot run: note it for the hand-over and go on. Where a command asks for a time span in angle brackets, give it the look-back above; where it asks for case ids in angle brackets, give it the ids of the cases you are working. Where a command reads only the last lines of a log (--tail), a line not found there rules its cause out only if the oldest line returned is older than the look-back time; if it is not, note the check for the hand-over as not fully run, and go on.
Group its cases by the state they are in (Submitted, Awaiting validation, Stock confirmed) and work each group below that has cases, the largest first.

Stage 2 runbook: Accept the order › Alert

Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed

No test of this runbook is on record.

A payment outage cancels every order that reaches Stock confirmed (“The order is cancelled because payment failed”), and none of them waits, so “Orders past the acceptance time limit, by state” stays flat while the shopper loses the order

It has been above the operators’ threshold for longer than their window (the alert).

Its cases those that left by “The order is cancelled because payment failed” from Stock confirmed in the alert's window. A case still in the stage is not one of this alert's.
Look back from when the earliest of its cases entered the stage, to now: what sent a case out wrongly can come before it left.
Do now
  1. List its cases and set the look-back. Every check below runs on these cases, over that time. List them with the alert’s own count:
    How

    Ordering-api log lines 'Handling integration event:' naming OrderPaymentFailedIntegrationEvent, one per order, searched over the window in the log store, against the orders that entered acceptance in it ("OrderDate" in ordering.orders)

  2. Contain. Stop more cases leaving by “The order is cancelled because payment failed”: no person makes these moves, so nothing here holds more cases back; they keep leaving until the cause is restored. “The order is cancelled because payment failed” cannot be undone: a case already left by it stays as it is.
  3. Do not set "OrderStatus" straight to 'StockConfirmed', 'Paid' or 'Cancelled' by SQL: the events are raised only inside the setters, so no outbox row is written and nothing after it happens (payment, stock reduction, notifications)
  4. Do not set an outbox row's "State" back to 0 to have it sent: nothing reads unsent rows after the request that wrote them
  5. Do not look for failed messages to replay: a consumer acknowledges a message it failed on, and no dead-letter queue exists
  6. Do not restart order-processor to move orders held in Awaiting validation or Stock confirmed: the poll selects only Submitted
  7. Do not restart the postgres or eventbus container apps as a first move: no data volume is declared for either, so find out where their data lives first
  8. Escalate or declare as soon as a trigger is met, at any point below. Triggers ›
Check first
1Is this already known?
How
Look for an open incident, or a known error with a fix in flight, for any of these parts: Order Processor, Ordering API, Ordering database, Event bus, Catalog API, Catalog database, Payment Processor, ClientApp, Mobile BFF, Identity API. Not the cause if there is none; the cause if one is open: link it and close.
Yes → Already known
2Was it planned?
How

Every run re-publishes for each order still Submitted. The bus's retry policy never retries a failed publish: Execute is given an async lambda, so the failure lands in the returned task, not the call; Process step 2.2: Stock is confirmed for every item of the order — 10 seconds of simulated work before the status is set. Ordering API consumes its queue with one consumer on one channel, so these waits queue behind one another; Other outcome: The order is cancelled because an item is out of stock — 10 seconds of simulated work before the status is set, queued behind the other waits as in “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order”; Expected outcome: Payment is taken for the order — 10 seconds of simulated work before the status is set, on the same single consumer as “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order”; Other outcome: The order is cancelled because payment failed — No wait and no timeout: unlike “Payment is taken for the order”, Ordering API sets Cancelled at once, but on the same single consumer as “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order”, so it queues behind the 10-second waits there. No clock watches a message waiting in its queue, and the queue sets no expiry; Other outcome: The order is cancelled at the customer's request — No timeout of its own: the mobile app's HttpClient has no handler, so it keeps .NET's default timeout of 100 seconds and makes one attempt; Mobile BFF's route and Ordering API's cancel endpoint set none, and the cancel itself waits for nothing). Not the cause if there is none; the cause if a window is open or a setting was changed on purpose: link it and close.
Yes → Planned change
3Did something change when it started?
How
Look for any deploy, configuration change or unplanned restart of those parts since the look-back time above. Not the cause if there is none; the cause if a change lines up with the start.
Yes → Roll the change back, or escalate to the owner of the part that changed

How
Read the alert's own count over one window. Not the cause if it is not falling; a falling count means only that no new cases are arriving, and the cases it counted stay wrong: this check never closes the alert, so go on and work them.
Yes → No new cases: go on and work the ones it counted

8Are the messages for Event bus accepted but routed to no queue?
How
How to check

In the eventbus container (az containerapp exec --name eventbus --resource-group <rg>) run rabbitmqctl list_bindings source_name destination_name routing_key, and read the rows whose source is eshop_event_bus.

Not the cause if Catalog bound for OrderStatusChangedToAwaitingValidationIntegrationEvent; PaymentProcessor for OrderStatusChangedToStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent; Ordering for OrderStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent, OrderStockRejectedIntegrationEvent, OrderPaymentSucceededIntegrationEvent and OrderPaymentFailedIntegrationEvent
The cause if One of those bindings missing
The same check in the reference ›
Yes → Restore: remedy 1
9Is Payment Processor failing to publish its messages?
How
How to check

Search the console log of payment-processor (az containerapp logs show --name payment-processor --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for 'Publishing integration event:' for the order followed by 'Error Processing message' for its OrderStatusChangedToStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent.

Not the cause if A 'Publishing integration event:' line and no error
The cause if The publishing line followed by 'Error Processing message'
The same check in the reference ›
Yes → Restore: remedy 1
10Is Payment Processor failing on the messages it reads?
How
How to check

Search the console log of payment-processor (az containerapp logs show --name payment-processor --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for 'Error Processing message' for OrderStatusChangedToStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent with no 'Publishing integration event:' line before it.

Not the cause if No such line
The cause if The error with no result published
The same check in the reference ›
Yes → Restore: remedy 1
11Are Ordering API and Catalog API failing to publish their messages?
How
How to check

Search the console log of ordering-api (az containerapp logs show --name ordering-api --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for 'Error publishing integration event:', and that of catalog-api the same way for 'Error Publishing integration event:', and read the exception each carries. Note which service logged it.

Not the cause if No such line in either service
The cause if Lines for these orders' events naming a broker or connection error; the service whose log holds them is the one that matched
The same check in the reference ›
Yes → Restore: remedy 1
12Are Ordering API's outbox rows marked failed?
How
How to check

In the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run:

psql -U postgres -d orderingdb

Then:

SELECT o."Id", o."OrderStatus", l."State", l."EventId" FROM ordering.orders o LEFT JOIN ordering."IntegrationEventLog" l ON (l."Content"::jsonb ->> 'OrderId')::int = o."Id" AND ((o."OrderStatus" = 'AwaitingValidation' AND l."EventTypeName" LIKE '%OrderStatusChangedToAwaitingValidationIntegrationEvent') OR (o."OrderStatus" = 'StockConfirmed' AND l."EventTypeName" LIKE '%OrderStatusChangedToStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent')) WHERE o."OrderStatus" IN ('AwaitingValidation','StockConfirmed') AND now() - o."OrderDate" > interval '2 minutes';

Then search the console log of ordering-api (az containerapp logs show --name ordering-api --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for 'Error publishing integration event:' with those EventIds.

Not the cause if "State" 2 (Published) on every row
The cause if "State" 3 (PublishedFailed), with the error line
The same check in the reference ›
Yes → Restore: remedy 1
